fact: Blood on the Clocktower was designed by Steven Medway and published by The Pandemonium Institute, after a 2018 Kickstarter that raised over $570,000 against a $65,000 goal.
The game won Tabletop Gaming's “Best Party Game” award in 2022, and was a runner-up for BoardGameGeek's Golden Geek Award the same year.
Unlike most social deduction games, dying here isn't leaving the table — the dead keep talking, and keep one last vote to spend for the rest of the game.
The person running the game is called the Storyteller, not a moderator — the job is narrating what the night did, not just enforcing rules.
The Grimoire is the Storyteller's own private record of who everyone really is — the one thing at the table nobody else ever gets to read.
“Registers as” is one of the game's load-bearing phrases — it means an ability can be fooled into treating a player as someone, or something, they aren't.
A drunk or poisoned player is never told their ability has stopped working — they use it exactly as if it were real, and so does everyone watching them.
There's a real touring stage show, Blood on the Clocktower: Live!, that turns an unscripted game into comedy theatre — it's played the Edinburgh Festival Fringe.
Good wins the instant the Demon dies. Evil wins the instant only two players are left alive. Nothing else ends the game.
The official scripts are built for anywhere from five to twenty players in one sitting — tonight's table sits right in the middle of that range.
A nomination needs support from more than half of everyone still alive to succeed — a tie, or a near-miss, executes no one.
Some characters can be quietly impaired without ever being the actual Drunk — a poisoned player believes their real ability is working just fine.
The Imp can choose to kill itself — do that, and a Minion silently inherits the demon's mantle for the rest of the game.
Killing a target the Imp already knows is dead is a completely legal move — a sharp Imp will sometimes burn a night's kill on a corpse just to protect its bluffs.
The Recluse is entirely good — but any detection ability in the game might be told by the Storyteller that they're a Minion, or even the Demon.
A Recluse's evil disguise never comes with any evil powers attached — it's a costume the Storyteller hands them, not a transformation.
The Spy is the only Minion who gets to read the Storyteller's actual Grimoire, every single night of the game.
A dead Spy still wakes to see the Grimoire — death switches off the body, not the ability.
The Virgin's ability only ever fires once, and only against a Townsfolk nominator — an Outsider, Minion, or Demon can nominate the Virgin completely safely.
A Fortune Teller's reading still works on a Demon who's already dead — asking about a corpse can be a perfectly legitimate move.
One good player in every game is secretly a “Red Herring” who will always look like the Demon to the Fortune Teller, whether either of them likes it or not.
The Baron's ability fires once, at setup, before a single card is even looked at — and it can never be undone, even if the Baron dies in the first minute.
If the Demon dies with five or more players still standing, the Scarlet Woman quietly becomes the new Demon — same powers, same win condition, brand new face.
The Undertaker only ever learns about executions — a night kill teaches them nothing, no matter how many people die.
What the Undertaker sees is the truth, not the belief — execute a drunk Townsfolk, and the Undertaker is told “Drunk,” not whatever that player thought they were.
The Zombuul gets to die once for free — it keeps killing at night, but every waking player treats it as a corpse from then on.
A Zombuul only strikes on nights that follow a day with no death at all — the quietest Demon in the game, right up until it isn't.
The Godfather knows every Outsider in the game from the very first night — before a single clue has reached anyone else.
Execute an Outsider, and the Godfather gets to kill that same night — good's own vote can hand evil its next victim.
